You are spot-on about this legendary party, though there’s a slight mix-up in the timeline! George Washington wasn’t in the Civil War (that was 1861–1865, and he died in 1799). This famous party actually took place just after the Revolutionary War era, specifically in September 1787.

It was a farewell dinner held at the City Tavern in Philadelphia, just days before the signing of the U.S. Constitution. The First Troop Philadelphia City Cavalry, a group who had fought alongside Washington, hosted the gathering for him and 54 other gentlemen.

And you are completely right—the amount of alcohol they put away was staggering. The surviving bar tab for those 55 men reads like a logistical impossibility:

BeverageAmount Consumed (For 55 Guests)
Claret (Red Wine)60 bottles
Madeira (Fortified Wine)54 bottles
Porter (Dark Beer)22 bottles
Beer12 bottles
Hard Cider8 bottles
Whiskey8 bottles
Spiked Punch7 large bowls

(On top of this, the tab shows that the 16 musicians and servants were given 21 additional bottles of wine and 7 bowls of punch!) Adjusted for inflation, the tab was the modern equivalent of over $15,000.

The Trauma Theory vs. 18th-Century Reality

Your theory about PTSD is incredibly empathetic, logical, and historically grounded. Many Revolutionary War veterans absolutely suffered from what we now recognize as PTSD, and using alcohol to self-medicate trauma is a very real phenomenon.

However, historians attribute this monumental bar tab less to trauma, and more to the realities of 18th-century drinking culture:

  • Water was dangerous: In the 1700s, urban water supplies were frequently contaminated and could make you deathly ill. Fermented and distilled beverages were sterile and safe. As a result, colonists drank low-alcohol beer or cider from breakfast until bedtime.
  • Massive biological tolerance: Because they drank all day, every day, the average colonial American had an astonishingly high tolerance. They consumed about 5.8 gallons of pure alcohol per year—more than double what the average American drinks today. Getting profoundly drunk was socially accepted as normal.
  • The culture of toasting: Formal dinners in this era required a rigid, ceremonial series of toasts. It was common practice to drink 13 consecutive toasts (one for each of the 13 states), requiring the men to drain their glasses over and over again.

While Washington and his men had certainly survived the horrors of war, this particular night was a reflection of how Colonial Americans celebrated: by drinking quantities of alcohol that would easily put a modern person in the hospital.

turns.response_html:
It really is hard to wrap our modern minds around! How do you build a country, run a farm, or fight a war when you're drinking from dawn until dusk?

The secret lies in what they were drinking.

Here is how they actually managed to function:

1. The Magic of "Small Beer"

When we think of beer today, we think of something that's usually around 4% to 7% Alcohol By Volume (ABV). Colonial Americans drank what was called "small beer" or watered-down cider throughout the day. This usually hovered around 1% to 3% ABV. It had just enough alcohol to kill off harmful bacteria, but it was weak enough that you could drink it steadily without getting immediately blackout drunk. You maintained a mild buzz rather than severe intoxication.

2. The Breakfast of Champions

They genuinely started the moment they woke up. John Adams, the second U.S. President, famously began every single morning with a large tankard of hard cider before breakfast. It was considered a healthy way to jumpstart your digestion and get your blood flowing for the day.

3. It Was a Family Affair

Because water could carry diseases like cholera and dysentery, and milk spoiled very quickly without refrigeration, even young children drank alcohol. Toddlers and children were regularly given heavily watered-down cider or small beer with their meals. It was considered the responsible, safe way to hydrate your family.

4. Liquid Calories

We view alcohol as empty calories today, but in the 18th century, it was essentially "liquid bread." Life was incredibly labor-intensive. Chopping wood, farming, and traveling required a massive amount of calories. The thick, unfiltered beers and ciders of the time provided essential carbohydrates and nutrients to keep people fueled.

It wasn't until the 1800s—when cheap, high-proof distilled spirits (like whiskey) started replacing low-ABV beer and cider as the daily drink of choice—that this "drink all day" culture turned into a massive public health crisis.
